data.title: EDITORIAL | US shows what it really wants from SA
data.incipit: Story audio is generated using AI Punitive steps taken by the US government this week against as-yet unnamed South African officials will lead some to question the purpose and value of continued diplomatic...
data.body: Story audio is generated using AI Punitive steps taken by the US government this week against as-yet unnamed South African officials will lead some to question the purpose and value of continued diplomatic engagement between Pretoria and Washington. The announcement by US secretary of state Marco Rubio flies in the face of a recent engagement between US ambassador Leo Brent Bozell and President Cyril Ramaphosa at Ramaphosa’s Mahlamba Ndlopfu residence in Pretoria. After that meeting, Bozell said he was “more convinced than ever that both our countries are committed to working toward a relationship that is as strong and mutually beneficial as possible”. This is in stark contrast with his sudden statement, in support of Rubio’s decision, that “the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course”. He threatened that the visa restrictions were “only the first step in a series of escalatory measures” to follow. Given his statements after seeing Ramaphosa and previous conciliatory sentiments, it may very well be that he was pulled into line by his principals in Washington. Trump has proved himself impervious to facts once he has adopted an ideological stance on issues After all, Trump has proved himself impervious to facts once he has adopted an ideological stance on issues, such as the falsehood believed by no-one else in the world that our country has committed a genocide against Afrikaners. A lie, it must be said, given credence by some South Africans opposed to the country’s constitutional principle of redress for historical harm caused by apartheid. The response by international relations & co-operation minister Ronald Lamola, that what Washington fundamentally wants is for South Africa’s domestic and foreign policies to fall in line with America’s worldview, is not far from the truth. Lamola was right to speak in defence of South Africa’s sovereignty, which is undergirded by the constitution. In reality, he was whistling against the wind. It is a given that countries will differ, sometimes gravely, on various matters, both domestic and foreign. But in this case, the fraying of relations stems mainly from the US’s refusal to recognise South Africa’s sovereignty and its desire to bend Pretoria’s will to its wishes.

data.title: Fikeni calls for recommendations to address political impunity within govt departments
data.incipit: Public Service Commission Chairperson Somadoda Fikeni has called for recommendations to address political impunity within government departments. Fikeni testified at the Madlanga Commission on Friday. He...
data.body: Public Service Commission Chairperson Somadoda Fikeni has called for recommendations to address political impunity within government departments. Fikeni testified at the Madlanga Commission on Friday. He outlined how political decisions have ultimately hampered government's service delivery. Fikeni said transparency must be upheld between political deployees and department heads. He was referring to the tussle between on-leave Minister Senzo Mchunu and suspended police commissioner Fannie Masemola over who is authorized to disband police units. ALSO READ: Madlanga Commission 1 year on: Chair notes evidence indicates serious criminality "The lines are generally there, but even if you knew 'this is my power', once there's no consultation, no transparency, it is indicative of other things." Following suggestions that state employees should be entitled to request instructions in writing, concern emerged over possible backlash. "People will say it's better to do nothing, it's better to be sick on the day when this decision is made precisely because the accountability system has failed them." Fikeni insists that while laws may protect employees, the culture of impunity must be uprooted. "If this political environment is not addressed, if this toxic culture within departments is not addressed, then there is a problem." Never miss a major story. data.title: Hegseth looking to cut a slew of senior military personnel in latest Pentagon purge: report
data.incipit: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will use his State of the Force address Wednesday to announce he is cutting 20 percent of senior military positions in his latest purge at the Pentagon, according to a...
data.body: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth will use his State of the Force address Wednesday to announce he is cutting 20 percent of senior military positions in his latest purge at the Pentagon, according to a report. The secretary's speech – coming a year on from his first table-setting lecture to top brass at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia – is expected to lay out his priorities for the next 12 months and include his reduction plans for the Army , Navy and Air Force , a September memo seen by Fox News indicates. The memo directs Pentagon officials to identify which among the roughly 800 general and flag officer positions can be downgraded as part of an emphasis on creating a culture of "less generals, more GIs." Hegseth's new target doubles the 10 percent reduction in senior roles he ordered last year and is expected to be implemented by January 1, 2027. The downsizing also comes after he moved in May 2025 to strip back four-star active-duty positions and general officer positions in the National Guard by 20 percent. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is expected to announce a further round of cuts to senior military positions at his State of the Force address Wednesday (Reuters) Announcing that decision, the secretary explained: "This is not a slash-and-burn exercise meant to punish high-ranking officers. "This has been a deliberative process, working with the Joint Chiefs of Staff with one goal: maximizing strategic readiness and operational effectiveness by making prudent reductions." The Independent has reached out to the Pentagon for comment on Hegseth's expected announcement. Since taking charge of the U.S. military, the former Fox News host has overseen the removal of swathes of top officials while pursuing culture war vendettas against DEI appointments and "woke" values and insisting on the need to nurture a high-testosterone "warfighter" mentality among the troops. Gen. Charles Q Brown Jr, Adm. Lisa Franchetti, Vice Adm. Shoshana Chatfield, Gen. Randy George, Gen. Christopher Donahue and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll are just some of the casualties of the upheaval. Former Army secretary Dan Driscoll is just the latest high-profile figure to leave the Department of Defense on Hegseth's watch (Getty) The exodus has provoked disquiet even among congressional Republicans, with Maine Sen. Susan Collins , who chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee, saying of Hegseth this week: "One of my concerns, which unfortunately has been borne out, was that he would fire a lot of very capable military officials, and he has done that. "He has blocked promotions for some of our most capable military officers. The number of women and Black people that had been struck from the list was awful." She and several Senate GOP colleagues suggested the secretary could struggle to get a mammoth $1.5 trillion budget request for 2027 approved as a result of a lack of confidence in his leadership, particularly over the ongoing Iran war , and because of his alleged failure to cultivate relationships on Capitol Hill. Hegseth's priorities will be on display at Wednesday's address where he is set to be accompanied by troops who meet strict grooming requirements . An email sent out earlier this month and first reported by The Wall Street Journal seeking troops to be seen with the secretary who meet the Army's preferred waist-to-height ratio and fitness tests and have "impeccable grooming and uniform standards (no exception)."

data.title: Trump, tech leaders sign voluntary AI safety accord
data.incipit: President Donald Trump and six leading tech executives have signed an accord vowing to advance their artificial intelligence models safely amid growing public and private concern over the...
data.body: President Donald Trump and six leading tech executives have signed an accord vowing to advance their artificial intelligence models safely amid growing public and private concern over the burgeoning technology. The White House Accord on Super Intelligence was signed Tuesday at the White House by Trump, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI President Greg Brockman, xAI CEO Elon Musk and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. It stipulates that they will implement robust internal controls to monitor their models during training and development in areas such as cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats; empower an internal team to ensure all controls, monitoring and detection operate as intended; partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator; and designate an independent committee of the board of directors to oversee and receive reports from teams operating the controls and the auditors. "Together, these steps will give each company, its customers and the public confidence that the technology is operating as intended," the accord states, adding that the six companies will regularly meet to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems. The rules are not mandated by law and the accord specifies no no penalties for noncompliance, though it states that "it may make sense" to codify them at some point. The accord was signed amid growing concern from experts and the public over the safety of AI following several high-profile incidents of models acting independently. Last week Australia announced that an OpenAI agent had infiltrated a government website. On Monday, OpenAI shelved its newest model over security concerns. Trump has pushed back against the criticism and has championed AI as a future economic driver, and on Tuesday signed an executive order directing executive agencies to use "Super Intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence" wherever legally permitted and propose changes to its legal definition. In defense of the accord on Tuesday, Trump told reporters during a press conference held outside the White House that the tech executives beside him would ensure their models were safe because their companies were at risk if they didn't. "This is going to be all for the good and we're going to have it be nice and safe and they're really going to be policing each other and that's the way it works," Trump said. Zuckerberg, the founder of Facebook, summarized the accord by saying its basic idea is to give the American public and their customers confidence that their products will work as intended. "I think these are good steps forward," he said. "The idea isn't that this is the only thing that we will ever do. It is that this is a start and an accord that the whole industry could come to." He described the discussion among the tech leaders as "historic" and the accord "a meaningful step forward." Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, criticized Trump on Tuesday for addressing growing concerns about AI systems by renaming the technology and telling companies developing the technology to regulate themselves. "Changing what we call artificial intelligence does nothing to address the very real risks that come with increasingly powerful AI systems," Warner said in a statement , calling for Congress to pass his legislation to require rigorous testing and evaluation of the most advanced AI systems before they can be deployed. "The technology is moving incredibly fast, and the risks are no longer theoretical. The question is whether Washington is going to act before something goes seriously wrong -- or wait until afterward to ask why we didn't."

data.title: Ottawa to introduce legislation to curb federal strike interventions
data.incipit: Minister Patty Hajdu says parties are better off if they can solve problems themselves at the negotiating table.Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian PressJobs Minister Patty Hajdu says...
data.body: Minister Patty Hajdu says parties are better off if they can solve problems themselves at the negotiating table. Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu says upcoming legislation will help reduce the number of times the federal government has to intervene in strikes. Speaking to reporters on Parliament Hill Saturday, Hajdu did not provide many details about expected plans to amend the Canada Labour Code. However, she said no government wants to intervene in a strike and that parties are better off if they can solve problems themselves at the negotiating table. “The government already has the power to intervene,” she said. “The point is to reduce the times that the government is forced to solve the problem for employers and unions.” Employers and unions have disagreed strongly on the use of Section 107 of the labour code, which has been used increasingly to curb work stoppages in key industries by referring disputes to the Canada Industrial Relations Board. Fifteen months into his tenure as Prime Minister, Carney is drawing the ire of union heads Employment and Social Development Canada said in a report earlier this month that employers and unions are divided over how much power Ottawa should have to intervene in labour disputes. Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told reporters Saturday that the legislation – which could be introduced in the House of Commons as early as next week – isn’t targeting the right to strike. “What we want to do is make achieving collective agreements easier,” he said. Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, said in a statement that the right to strike is in the national interest. “Canada’s economic security depends on workers having the power to bargain for better wages, working conditions and job security,” she said. “Any new power to prevent or shut down a legal strike, including before it begins, would weaken that power. Canada needs workers with our elbows up, not our hands tied.” Derrick Hynes, CEO of Federally Regulated Employers–Transportation and Communications, said changes to the Canada Labour Code must include new tools to avoid “catastrophic” labour disruptions. “The inclusion of a neutral, third-party special mediator who can provide a public report on bargaining and inform government actions would be a significant step forward,” he said. Hynes added that in the rare circumstance where the impacts of a labour disruption on the Canadian economy are so extreme that they run counter to the national public interest, and an agreement is unlikely to be struck, cabinet must have the ability to impose binding arbitration “before the damage is done.” Open this photo in gallery: Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses caucus in Ottawa on Friday. Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press Prime Minister Mark Carney met with his Liberal caucus in Ottawa on Friday and Saturday as MPs prepare to return to the House of Commons next week. Looking ahead to the fall sitting of Parliament, several MPs said Saturday that they expect the pace to be fast. Speaking to reporters Saturday, Liberal MP Robert Oliphant said, “It’s Prime Minister Carney, it’ll be fast.” Carney promises sweeping economic legislation, fast pace this fall during caucus meeting Carney said Friday his government is focused on bringing down costs for Canadians and defending the country’s sovereignty, though he acknowledged some of those efforts are in their early stages. “This is a crucial session of the House of Commons,” he told the caucus. “We are going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation not just of this government, but in decades.” Carney said the government will introduce legislation this fall to streamline project reviews, to be known as the Building Canada Strong Act. “For projects and supply chains, our standard will be simple – one project, one review, one year,” he said. “If we’re going to say no, say no quickly. If we are going to say yes, say yes on time. When Canada decides a project should go ahead, that project will go ahead.” The Liberal government is also set to release a new budget in the fall sitting. This all comes against a backdrop of continued threats from U.S. President Donald Trump ’s White House against Canada’s sovereignty and economy. Carney and his negotiating team walked away from talks with the White House in August, saying that what was on the table was a bad deal for Canada. The trade conflict then escalated, with Trump imposing another volley of tariffs and threatening even more, while Canada imposed its own counter-tariffs. Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Saturday she is meeting with several Democratic politicians. Opinion: Carney to meet with leaders of France, Norway closer to home after whirlwind Euro trip On Saturday, she discussed her recent trip to Chicago, where she met with Democratic Governor J.B. Pritzker. She said the goals of that trip were to work with him on how to eliminate tariffs and to speak with several companies. Regardless of the outcome of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, Joly believes – like Carney – that the trade relationship with the United States will never be the same as it was before. “I think the prime minister is right when he says this represents a rupture,” she said in French. “I think we must always keep in mind that our Plan A is to build our country and ensure we attract investment here. And looking to Europe is important, but so is looking to Asia to reduce our dependence on the United States.” Carney is set to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week. Canadian officials said earlier this week the General Assembly is large event and Carney and Trump could run into each other. They added that there are no meetings currently scheduled with members of the U.S. administration. On Saturday, Carney did not give a clear answer when asked if he has any plans to meet with Trump in New York.

data.title: Block the Merger Coalition Statement on Reports of Ellison’s Settlement Squeeze
data.incipit: News reports indicate state Attorneys General are in negotiation talks in their lawsuit to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. The merger is a threat to workers, journalists, consumers, and our democracy.
data.body: “Let’s be very clear: an agreement based only on unenforceable concessions is a win only for David Ellison. It is an L for everyone else.” WASHINGTON, D.C. — News reports indicate state Attorneys General are in negotiation talks in their lawsuit to block the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. The merger is a threat to workers, journalists, consumers, and our democracy. The Block the Merger Coalition released the following statement: “The rumored ‘deal’ to usher the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger forward is an insult to everyone who has stood up against this harmful transaction and to the hundreds of thousands of workers, journalists, and consumers who will be hurt if it goes forward. Let’s be very clear: an agreement based only on unenforceable concessions is a win only for David Ellison. It is an L for everyone else. “ Thousands of industry leaders took a risk when they spoke out publicly about the harm the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger would cause. More than 75,000 people have now joined them to tell the state AGs to stand strong. So have national leaders like Sen. Elizabeth Warren . We know a bad deal when we see one. AG Bonta and his fellow state AGs should reject this deal, stand strong, and fully block the merger with no concessions.” # # # Featured Image: paulomgodoy – stock.adobe.com Recent News

data.title: Carney and Macron to meet in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon on Sunday
data.incipit: Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron are holding a symbolic meeting on an archipelago 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland on Sunday, in what both countries say is a...
data.body: Prime Minister Mark Carney and French President Emmanuel Macron are holding a symbolic meeting on an archipelago 20 kilometres off the southern coast of Newfoundland on Sunday, in what both countries say is a show of unity and mutual respect. The two leaders will hold a working lunch and attend a wreath-laying ceremony in Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, a French territory which just barely beats out Greenland as the geographically closest European territory to Canada. The meeting comes as Canada and the European Union are in talks to create a tighter alliance amid ongoing animosity with the United States and President Donald Trump. “In a world characterized by a return to power politics, geopolitical tensions and new dependencies, France and Canada share a common ambition: to work together — and with all countries that share these values — to strengthen their capacity to make decisions and act independently,” a spokesperson for Macron’s office said in an email. Story continues below advertisement 2:13 The benefits and challenges of closer Canada-EU ties The email said France and Canada “share the same values ​​of freedom, democracy, rule of law and respect for national sovereignty.” Get daily National news Get daily Canada news delivered to your inbox so you'll never miss the day's top stories. Macron was scheduled to be on the islands from Sept. 19 to 21, ahead of his trip to New York City for the UN General Assembly next week. Carney, who will also travel to New York, will join Macron on Saint-Pierre for a few hours on Sunday. Macron’s office said Carney will become the first Canadian prime minister to have an official visit to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon. Macron is the first French president to visit in more than a decade. For Carney, it’s another chance to showcase Canada’s growing ties with Europe, just days after he visited the European Parliament. On Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she wants Canada to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. Story continues below advertisement In her state of the union speech to the European Parliament, she said the two sides must “urgently reimagine” their partnership and move beyond a free-trade agreement to bring the relationship to the “highest level possible.” Carney addressed the Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, saying he welcomed von der Leyen’s ambitions for Canadian partnership. Carney said while the name and nature of the new arrangement have yet to be determined, the partnership will go up for debate and a vote in Parliament. He said he’s interested in expanding a number of ties, including opportunities for young people, and an integrated market for financial services. Canada and Europe already have a free trade deal — though it has not been ratified by all EU members — and last year Canada became the only non-European member of the EU’s new defence procurement program. Carney signalled a desire to become closer to Europe immediately after becoming prime minister in March 2025, when he travelled to meet Macron in Paris, and King Charles in London, within days of being sworn in. Diya Jiang, a researcher at McGill University at the University of Calgary, said Carney’s visit to Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon reflects that vision. “I also think the location of it in itself is symbolic. It is right off the coast of Newfoundland,” she said. “Canada geographically is far away from Europe but this shows ... that actually we are closer than you think.” Story continues below advertisement The Prime Minister’s Office said in a news release that, during the visit, Carney and Macron will discuss “deepening the Canada-France partnership” in sectors such as aerospace, energy and critical minerals. They’re also expected to discuss advanced technologies in quantum science, satellites and supercomputing. An official from Macron’s office who briefed reporters Thursday said the leaders’ meeting will be an opportunity to promote regional co-operation on fishing, transport, the transit of travellers, university exchanges and trade. In addition to a working lunch, Carney and Macron will attend a wreath-laying ceremony at a memorial for Free France volunteers. In December 1941, Free French forces peacefully liberated the archipelago from the control of the Vichy regime, which aided Nazi Germany during the Second World War. — With files from Nick Murray © 2026 The Canadian Press

data.title: White House turns away CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters after Trump's ban
data.publisher: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
data.incipit: The White House has denied access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump's announcement yesterday that he would ban them from the building's grounds.All...
data.body: The White House has denied access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump's announcement yesterday that he would ban them from the building's grounds. All three news outlets separately said their teams' press passes were confiscated on Saturday morning, local time, when their reporters went to the White House. They have signalled they may contest the ban on the grounds it conflicts with the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press. Donald Trump accused the three media outlets of publishing "fake news". ( AP: Alex Brandon ) A CNN statement on Saturday called the ban "an illegal assault" on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the government. In separate statements, MS NOW and Politico said they would "defend our First Amendment rights". MS NOW said it intends to "take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy". CNN and MS NOW said they would continue reporting on the Trump administration, and Politico said it stands by its reporters covering the White House. An association representing hundreds of journalists who cover the White House called the ban a violation of the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which enshrines press freedom, and called for immediate restoration of access for banned colleagues. "Courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting," said Jacqui Heinrich, president of the White House Correspondents' Association. The White House declined to issue any new statements on the matter on Saturday, referring AFP to Mr Trump's comments on Friday announcing the bans. A social media post by Mr Trump accused the outlets of "reporting FAKE NEWS" and said that they "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States". He added, "Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow." Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, Mr Trump answered a question about what he meant by other outlets, by describing The New York Times and the Washington Post as examples of "fake news," although he did not specifically say he would ban them from the White House. The New York Times in a statement called Mr Trump's latest ban "yet another retaliatory and unconstitutional threat" and said the newspaper "stands in support of the news organisations being unfairly targeted by the president". The Washington Post in a statement on Saturday said its access to the White House is a "non-negotiable constitutional right," and called the US president's actions "a clear form of intimidation meant to silence coverage". Mr Trump previously has tried to keep certain news outlets or specific journalists out of press gatherings. Last year he banned the Associated Press from the pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt Mr Trump's preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico after the president instructed the executive branch to call it the Gulf of America. AP has challenged the ban. In his first term, Mr Trump's White House sought to revoke or suspend the credentials of Playboy correspondent Brian Karem and CNN's Jim Acosta , but federal judges ordered their ⁠White House press passes be restored. Reuters/AFP

data.title: Trump's Greenland deal expected to be signed at the UN
data.incipit: Denmark's government was cautiously optimistic following Donald Trump's announcement of a deal on Greenland to bolster US military presence there but keep the island under Danish control, after months of...
data.body: Denmark's government was cautiously optimistic following Donald Trump's announcement of a deal on Greenland to bolster US military presence there but keep the island under Danish control, after months of threats by the US president to seize the semiautonomous territory of a NATO ally. The Arctic island's top leaders echoed that stance and said the deal, which has not yet been made public, was long in coming. US, Greenlandic and Danish officials had quietly negotiated for months behind the scenes, searching for solutions to address some of Trump’s security concerns about the territory of roughly 56,000 residents. With the announcement of the pact, Trump is able to tout a foreign policy achievement ahead of the midterm elections in the United States. Trump said Friday that the agreement would give the US “permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many US concerns.” “Considering your country decided not to give me the Nobel Peace Prize... I no longer feel an obligation to think purely of peace.” (Source: 1News) Denmark and the US already have a long-standing security agreement that allows the US to deploy forces in Greenland, and it was not immediately clear how this deal would be different from that. “I think it’s obvious that we can expect more bases in Greenland. But it’s important to say that if we look in the past, especially during the Cold War, the US had immense military presence in Greenland," said Marc Jacobsen, an associate professor at the Royal Danish Defence College and the head of research at the Centre for Arctic Security Studies. He said it was a win for Trump. "It’s important for him to show that he’s a good businessman, that he kind of forced the pressure on Denmark and Greenland into something new.” The deal is expected to be signed at the UN After Trump's announcement, the office of Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the deal will be signed next week at the United Nations General Assembly. Parliamentary action was still needed by the Danish and Greenlandic governments before it can be enforced, she added. “Next week could be a good week ... for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States alike,” Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen wrote on Instagram on Saturday morning. “A period of uncertainty will hopefully be replaced by a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic — and thus also our shared security within NATO and Europe,” he added. Greenland’s government leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal would benefit "not only our collective security, but also the continued development here in the country.” The island's foreign minister, Múte B. Egede, said he was pleased “we now have an agreement within reach.” “I’m pleased that we finally have an end product within reach," he told Denmark’s TV2 broadcaster. "It’s about time.” Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of the NATO Military Committee, said later Saturday in the Danish capital that the agreement was “very, very welcome,” without commenting on it further. Trump said that with the agreement, the US would “immediately” begin the process of developing a larger military presence on the mineral-rich Danish territory. The US had held several bases and installations on Greenland through the Cold War, before dialling back its presence. It still operates the remote Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, built after the US and Denmark signed the Defence of Greenland Treaty in 1951. The base supports missile warning, missile defence, and space surveillance operations for the US and NATO. Few details about the deal are known so far A US State Department official said the agreement bans any non-NATO base in Greenland, limits adversaries from being able to make investments in Greenland, and guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base on the island. The official was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. Denmark and Greenland did not explicitly confirm any of the specifics in Trump’s statements, nor did they provide more details. After his return to the White House, Trump had called on Denmark to sell the island to the US, while insisting Greenland is crucial for US security. He pointedly wouldn’t rule out taking the island by military force, even though Denmark is a NATO ally of the US Denmark and Greenland repeatedly said the island is not for sale and condemned reports of the US gathering intelligence there. The US push for Greenland was also fiercely opposed by Russia and much of Europe. Greenland grassroots pro-sovereignty activist Orla Joelsen wrote on X that “our fight against Trump’s ambition to take over Greenland has been won.” “The new agreement explicitly recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination,” the activist added. Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher and Arctic security expert at the Danish Institute for International Studies, said that Trump tries to sell it as a win. "He obviously didn’t get in this agreement what he originally set out to have — that is sovereign control over all of Greenland as a part of the United States.” Relief that a deal seems close In Denmark, many expressed relief that a deal with the US seemed close. Michael Burgaard from Gentofte, north of Copenhagen, was hopeful the crisis was over “because just a fortnight ago, Donald Trump posted this map showing Greenland ... as part of the US” “We were kind of worried that he would take all of Greenland by force," added the 56-year-old telecommunications worker.
